Most of what any of us believes about public affairs arrives secondhand. We do not see the negotiations, the harvests, or the battles; we read about them, and the report is shaped by those who wrote it and by our own habits of attention. Each person therefore carries a small picture of the world that is partly accurate and partly assembled from prior expectation. When the picture is challenged, we tend to defend it, because it is tied to our sense of who we are. This is not stupidity; it is economy. A mind that rebuilt its whole map at every headline would never act at all. But the consequence is that public opinion rests less on facts than on the images through which facts are received, and anyone who wishes to understand politics must begin by studying those images.
